children.value: Provide information about your character and the part of the world connected to them.
Brief answers are sufficient. One or two sentences per entry are usually enough.
Please try to fill in at least one point per section, but nothing is absolutely mandatory. Unknown or undecided details may be left blank and developed later during play.
Everything submitted is a proposal. The DM decides whether, how much, and in what form it becomes part of the setting or campaign. Ideas may be adapted, combined, delayed, or omitted.
Avoid establishing major historical events, world-famous people, powerful organisations, unique magical objects, or setting-wide truths without discussing them with the DM first.
Mark anything especially important to your character or enjoyment like this:
Such notes will be treated as priorities for discussion, but the DM has the final word on their inclusion and implementation.
Origin - What culture or community raised me?:
Former livelihood - What did I do before becoming an adventurer?:
Class hook - How did I gain, discover, or develop my abilities?:
Party hook - Why did I join the party?:
Inciting incident - Why did I leave my former life and begin adventuring now?:
Reason to stay - Why do I remain with the party after the first mission?:
Contribution - What do I bring to the party beyond combat?:

This section provides a small part of the world that may be used during the campaign.
Keep it local and playable. You do not need to design an entire kingdom.

Avoid establishing an exact position on the world map. Instead of terms such as "far west" or "east of the capital," describe the general environment: coast, forest, mountains, desert, plains, frostlands, swamp, river valley, borderland, or similar.
Environment - coast, forest, mountain, desert, plains, frost, swamp, or other:

They may be within your hometown or elsewhere in the surrounding region.

Suitable locations include a mill, ferry crossing, shrine, cemetery, workshop, inn, mine, fishing cove, abandoned watchtower, ruined bridge, warehouse, communal oven, orchard, quarry, market square, or roadside monument.
Behaviour locals consider shameful, strange, or suspicious:
A faction may be a family, guild, business, temple, patrol, militia, criminal crew, workers' group, political office, or informal community.
Add one to three small problems suitable for a level 1-3 party.
Problems should be local and manageable. They should not require the party to defeat an army, overthrow an empire, or save the entire world.
They may be solved through investigation, negotiation, exploration, stealth, practical work, or combat.
supplies disappearing along a local road.
Rumours may be true, false, exaggerated, or misunderstood.
For each NPC, place, object, or unresolved event, add a one-line problem that could become a side quest or plot hook.
